title: Symphony No. 3 (Beethoven)
wiki_lead:
The Symphony No. 3 in E♭ major, Op. 55, titled as the Eroica Symphony, is a symphony in four movements by Ludwig van Beethoven.
One of Beethoven's most celebrated works, the Eroica symphony is a large-scale composition that marked the beginning of the composer's innovative "middle period".
Composed mainly in 1803–1804, the work broke boundaries in symphonic form, length, harmony, emotional and cultural content. It is widely considered a landmark in the transition between the Classical and the Romantic era. It is also often considered to be the first Romantic symphony. Beethoven first conducted a private performance on 9 June 1804, and later the first public performance on 7 April 1805.

The Symphony No. 3 in E♭ major, Op. 55, titled as the Eroica Symphony, is a symphony in four movements by Ludwig van Beethoven.
One of Beethoven's most celebrated works, the Eroica symphony is a large-scale composition that marked the beginning of the composer's innovative "middle period".
Composed mainly in 1803–1804, the work broke boundaries in symphonic form, length, harmony, emotional and cultural content. Form

The work is in 4 movements:

Depending upon the conductor's style and observation of the exposition repeat in the first movement, the typical performance time is between 45 and 55 minutes.


I. Allegro con brio

The 1st movement, in 34 time, is in sonata form, with typical performances between 12 and 18 minutes long depending on interpretation and whether the exposition repeat is played. Unlike the longer adagio introductions in Beethoven's first two symphonies, the movement opens with two loud E♭ major chords, played by the whole orchestra, that establish the tonality of the movement.
The conductor Kenneth Woods has noted that the opening movement of Eroica was inspired by and modeled on Mozart's Symphony No. 39, and shares many attributes of that earlier symphony which precedes this one by a decade and a half.


Exposition

The exposition has three thematic groups with varying interpretations of functionality.

First group (measures 3 to 44, E♭ major)
Second group (measures 45 to 83, B♭ major)
Third group (measures 84 to 155, B♭ major)
The exposition begins with the cellos introducing the first theme. By the fifth bar of the melody (m. 7), a chromatic note (C♯) is introduced, thus introducing the harmonic tension of the work. The melody is finished by the first violins, with a syncopated series of Gs (which forms a tritone with C♯ of the cellos and a diminished chord). This resolves to the dominant of the relative minor (G/C minor) before a short cadential codetta in E♭ major. The first theme is then transferred to wind instruments, then fragmented, moving through other keys with the b motif in canon and interchanged with a hemiola in the dominant, later moving between dominant and tonic. The main theme is finally restated with full orchestra in a and b before modulating to F major and the dominant B♭ in group 2.

The modulation to the dominant key of B♭ appears at mm. 42 to 44, although it is not yet fully stabilized and entrenched. Here follows a group of three or two subjects: a lyrical downward motif (mm. 45 to 56) in canon between oboe, clarinet, flute, and violin; a short upward scale motif (mm. 57 to 64) in strings with a variation; and a section beginning with rapid downward patterns in the violins (mm. 65 to 82).
The third theme of the second group eventually leads to a lyrical theme (m. 83), whose second half of the theme eventually builds to a loud melody (m. 109) that draws upon the earlier downward motif (m. 113). The climactic moment of the exposition arrives when the music is interrupted by 6 consecutives sforzando hemiola chords (mm. 128 to 131). Later, and following the concluding chords of the exposition (mm. 144 to 148), the main theme returns in a brief codetta (m. 148) that transitions into the repeat / development.
The status of these groups is debated as to which is more important in the structure. In the traditional analysis, the three early motifs are transitional subjects to arrive at the "unusually late" lyrical theme. An alternative analysis holds that the second theme begins earlier at m. 45 with the downward motif. In this view, the traditional harmonic progression of the exposition ends at m. 82, with the new lyrical theme at m. 83 beginning an extension. This
grok_lead: The Symphony No. 3 in E-flat major, Op. 55, known as the Eroica ("heroic"), is a four-movement orchestral work composed by Ludwig van Beethoven primarily between 1803 and 1804. Originally conceived as a tribute to Napoleon Bonaparte, reflecting Beethoven's admiration for the revolutionary ideals he embodied, the symphony's title page bore a dedication to "Buonaparte" until Beethoven, upon hearing of Napoleon's 1804 self-coronation as emperor, violently erased it in disillusionment, reportedly declaring that Napoleon would now "tread on the rights of man " like any tyrant. Rededicated to Prince Franz Joseph von Lobkowitz, a key patron, it received a private premiere at his Vienna palace in 1804 and a public one in 1805, where its unprecedented lengthânearly double that of typical contemporary symphoniesâand bold innovations elicited mixed reactions, with some auditors finding it bewilderingly complex. Comprising an expansive sonata-form first movement ( Allegro con brio), a profound funeral march ( Marcia funebre: Adagio assai), a vigorous scherzo ( Scherzo: Allegro vivace), and a finale of variations on a Prometheus ballet theme ( Finale: Allegro molto), the Eroica broke from Classical norms through extended developments, dynamic contrasts, and thematic transformations that evoke heroic struggle and resolution. This symphony heralded Beethoven's "heroic" middle period, revolutionizing the genre by prioritizing emotional narrative and structural ambition over balance, profoundly shaping Romantic symphonism and subsequent orchestral composition.
